newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel still sees chance of tax compromise.
newsitem.headline: Waigel still sees chance of tax compromise.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in an interview released on Saturday that he still saw chances for a tax compromise with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

But SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine accused the government of trying to conceal from voters a "vast tax increase programme" from 1999 onwards to cover a revenue shortfall of 60 billion marks ($35 billion).
The government needs SPD cooperation to carry out its plans for a sweeping fiscal reform since the SPD has the power to block most of the measures with its majority in the Upper House of parliament.

But talks between the two sides aimed at securing a consensus collapsed last Wednesday, consigning the tax measures to a tortuous passage through parliament and a likely deadlock in a parliamentary arbitration panel.

According to an advance release from Sunday's weekly Bild am Sonntag, Waigel said there was scope for agreement on the government's proposals for a bottom tax rate of 15 percent and a peak rate of 35 percent on corporate tax.
"A sensible peak rate for private income follows almost automatically from that," Waigel said.
He also said there was scope for compromise on government proposals, vehemently opposed by the SPD, to cut tax breaks on shift and night-time work.
But Lafontaine accused the government of delaying its tax reform until 1999 to hide planned tax increases.
"Kohl's government is planning a drastic increase in value added tax and petrol tax to finance its tax reform," Lafontaine told the daily Suedkurier.

Lafontaine repeated his allegation that Waigel would have to cover a shortfall of 56 billion marks for 1999 under current tax forecasts, and that this would grow beyond 60 billion when tax revenue estimates are released next month.
He said Waigel planned to add 20 pfennigs -- around 12 percent -- to the price of a litre of petrol and raise value added tax by two points to 17 percent.

In the talks which collapsed last week, the two sides come close to agreeing to cut the bottom rate of income tax and reduce corporation tax. The main sticking point was Waigel's plan to cut the top rate of income tax to 39 percent in 1999 from 53 percent.
The SPD also fundamentally opposed the government's Anglo-Saxon style supply-side approach to encourage corporate investment.
The SPD demanded above all that a big cut in non-wage labour costs -- unemployment, health and pensions insurance charges -- be made this summer to boost consumer demand.
-- Kevin Liffey, Bonn newsroom +49-228-26097160 ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
